opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the distinction we draw today is mostly an artifact of where the hardware is right now, not something fundamental.

If you think about what UMI actually is, it's a handheld gripper with a camera on it. A human holds it, does the task, and you record what the gripper sees and how it moves. The whole point is to put a human in the loop, but strip away the parts of the human that the robot can't use. The human provides the intelligence and the motion, and the device makes sure the observation and action spaces line up with the robot's embodiment. So you trade some naturalness for alignment.

Human data, like egocentric video from glasses or wrist cameras, sits at the other end. It's very natural and very scalable, because people are just living their lives, but there's a big embodiment gap: human hands versus robot grippers, different viewpoints, no clean action labels.

What I see happening is that the two ends are moving toward each other. On the UMI side, people want devices that are lighter, less intrusive, and closer to how you'd naturally use your hands, because that's how you get scale and diversity. On the human data side, we're adding more sensing, like better hand tracking, wrist cameras, sometimes tactile gloves, and we're getting much better at retargeting human motion onto robots and learning representations that bridge the embodiment gap.

At some point you end up with someone wearing lightweight sensors and doing everyday tasks naturally, and the data is rich enough and well aligned enough that a robot can learn directly from it. Is that UMI or human data? It doesn't really matter anymore. It's just human demonstration data with the right instrumentation.

And the robots are converging too. As hands get more dexterous and more humanoid, the embodiment gap shrinks from the robot side as well. So I think the long-term picture is a continuum, not two separate paradigms. The real question is how we capture human behavior at scale with enough fidelity that a robot can use it, and UMI and human video are two early points along that same path.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to look at it is to ask what UMI actually is. It's a hand-held gripper with a camera on it, and a person operates it directly. So mechanically you already have a human in the loop generating the motion. The difference between that and a pure human video is really just the end effector and the observation. In UMI the end effector is a parallel-jaw gripper and the camera is mounted on the wrist. In human data the end effector is a hand and the camera is wherever the recording device happens to be.

Now, both of those gaps are closing from both directions. On the hardware side, the grippers people are building for these hand-held devices are getting more dexterous, and at the same time the robot hands people are deploying are converging toward something you can actually wear or hold. So the morphology gap shrinks. On the perception side, the models are getting quite good at abstracting away the embodiment. If you train on enough egocentric video, the policy learns about object affordances, contact, how things move when you push them, and it stops caring very much whether the thing doing the pushing is a finger or a jaw. We already see that in retargeting work, where you can take hand pose and map it to a gripper or a dexterous hand and lose surprisingly little.

And then there's the data side. UMI's big contribution, in my view, wasn't the gripper itself. It was showing that you could collect robot-usable data without a robot in the room. That's exactly the appeal of human data too. So the two are solving the same problem, which is: how do you get demonstrations at scale without being bottlenecked by expensive robots and teleop rigs. When two approaches are solving the same problem with the same source of motion, which is a human body, the distinction eventually becomes an implementation detail.

So my prediction is that in a few years you won't talk about "UMI data" versus "human data." You'll talk about human-generated demonstration data, with some metadata about what the end effector looked like and how good the pose tracking was. The model will handle the rest. The thing that will actually matter is coverage, how diverse the tasks and environments are, not which device was in the person's hand.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is mostly about how we collect the data today. With UMI, you give a person a device that makes their actions easier to translate into robot actions. With human video, you have to infer more of that information—how the hand is moving, what it’s touching, and what forces might be involved.

But underneath, you’re observing the same thing: a person interacting with the physical world to accomplish a task. As our models get better at extracting that structure, the particular interface used to collect it should matter less. You want the model to learn what happens when you grasp something, move it, or make contact, across different hands and embodiments.

So I don’t mean the raw data will literally become identical. I mean that, from the learning system’s perspective, they can become complementary observations of the same underlying behavior. UMI gives you a more direct signal today; human data gives you much broader coverage. Eventually, I expect we’ll learn from both within the same framework.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction will become less important as we get better at extracting what matters from the data. With UMI, you have a device that makes the human demonstration easier to translate into something a robot can execute. With ordinary human video, you have to infer more—what the hand is doing, how it’s interacting with the object, and how that maps onto the robot.

But ultimately, both are observations of someone accomplishing a task. If we can recover the relevant motion and interaction well enough, they can provide the same kind of learning signal. UMI gives us a more direct bridge today. Over time, I expect the models to learn more of that bridge themselves, so the boundary between those data sources starts to disappear.
